voipred.dev evaluates a prediction model in a validation sample in two steps:

  1. nb() computes the net benefit of the model, of treating everyone and of treating no one, at each risk threshold;
  2. plot_dca() draws the decision curve, or the gain of the model over the best default strategy (\(\Delta NB\)).

The outcome decides the analysis: a binary outcome (part 1), or a survival or competing-risks outcome (part 2). Part 3 lists the models voipred can use by itself, and shows how to use any other model.

This vignette explains each option briefly, with examples. The help pages give the full details: ?nb, ?plot_dca, ?cipcw_control and ?predict_risk.

Installation

voipred.dev and bayespred are installed from GitHub; the other packages used in this vignette are on CRAN (survival and ggplot2 come with voipred.dev). Packages you already have are not installed again; voipred.dev is always reinstalled, to get its latest version:

pkgs <- c("remotes", "ranger", "e1071", "riskRegression", "prodlim")
new <- pkgs[!vapply(pkgs, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(new)) install.packages(new)
if (!requireNamespace("bayespred", quietly = TRUE))
  remotes::install_github("resplab/bayespred")
remotes::install_github("amirfarahmand0/voipred_dev", force = TRUE)   # voipred.dev
library(voipred.dev)
library(survival)

Part 1: binary outcome

Data

The GUSTO-I trial data ships with the package. The outcome is 30-day mortality (day30). We fit the models on a development sample and evaluate them on a separate validation sample.

set.seed(1)
i   <- sample(nrow(gusto))
dev <- gusto[i[1:5000], ]
val <- gusto[i[5001:10000], ]

mean(val$day30)   # prevalence in the validation sample
#> [1] 0.0692

Net benefit of one model

fit_glm <- glm(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
               family = binomial, data = dev)

res_glm <- nb(fit_glm, data = val, outcome = "day30",
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01), label = "Logistic")
res_glm
#> Net benefit of Logistic: n = 5000, prevalence = 0.0692, 31 thresholds
#>  threshold    NB_model        NB_all NB_none     delta_NB
#>       0.00 0.069200000  0.0692000000       0 0.0000000000
#>       0.01 0.060791919  0.0597979798       0 0.0009939394
#>       0.02 0.052857143  0.0502040816       0 0.0026530612
#>       0.03 0.047125773  0.0404123711       0 0.0067134021
#>       0.04 0.041750000  0.0304166667       0 0.0113333333

#>       0.11 0.019200000 -0.0458426966       0 0.0192000000

The result has one row per threshold:

  • NB_model: net benefit of treating the patients whose predicted risk is at or above the threshold;
  • NB_all: net benefit of treating everyone;
  • NB_none: net benefit of treating no one (always 0);
  • delta_NB: \(NB_{model} - \max(NB_{all}, NB_{none})\), the gain of the model over the best default strategy. The model is useful where it is positive.

Plots

plot_dca() draws the decision curve (type = "nb", the default) or delta_NB (type = "delta"):

plot_dca(res_glm)

plot_dca(res_glm, type = "delta")

Comparing models

Compute nb() for each model on the same data and thresholds, then give all the results to plot_dca():

fit_rf <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                         data = dev, probability = TRUE, num.trees = 500, seed = 1)
res_rf <- nb(fit_rf, val, "day30", thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01),
             label = "Random forest")

library(bayespred)
fit_bpm <- bpmfit(day30 ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse + pmi + miloc + sex,
                  data = dev, prior = log_f(m = 2))
res_bpm <- nb(fit_bpm, val, "day30", thresholds = seq(0, 0.30, by = 0.01),
              label = "Bayesian logistic")

plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm)

plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, res_bpm, type = "delta")

For the bayespred model the risk is the posterior mean of risk.

Options of nb() for a binary outcome

Argument What it does
model The fitted model. voipred gets the predicted risks from it (part 3). A vector of risks is not accepted.
data The validation sample. It must contain every covariate the model uses.
outcome The binary outcome: a column name ("day30"), a vector, or a formula (~ day30); 0/1, logical, or a two-level factor.
thresholds Risk thresholds in [0, 1). Default seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01). A patient is treated when the risk is at or above the threshold.
weights Optional case weights, one per patient (sampling weights, or a bootstrap draw).
predict_function Optional: your own function that returns the predicted risks (part 3).
label Name of the model in printed output and plots. Default: the name of the model object.

See ?nb for the details of each argument.

Weights. An integer weight counts a patient that many times, so bootstrap draws can be made without copying the data. The weights of an ordinary bootstrap are the number of times each patient is drawn; those of a Bayesian bootstrap are Dirichlet(1, …, 1):

n <- nrow(val)
z <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
set.seed(2)
w_boot <- tabulate(sample(n, replace = TRUE), nbins = n)
w_bb   <- rexp(n); w_bb <- n * w_bb / sum(w_bb)

draws <- rbind(original  = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z)$NB_model,
               bootstrap = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_boot)$NB_model,
               bayesian  = nb(fit_glm, val, "day30", z, weights = w_bb)$NB_model)
colnames(draws) <- paste("z =", z)
round(draws, 4)
#>           z = 0.02 z = 0.05 z = 0.1 z = 0.2
#> original    0.0529   0.0383  0.0218  0.0080
#> bootstrap   0.0470   0.0334  0.0179  0.0048
#> bayesian    0.0525   0.0388  0.0237  0.0103

Checks. voipred stops with a clear message when the risks cannot be right. Some examples:

# a covariate is missing from the validation data
nb(fit_glm, val[, setdiff(names(val), "sysbp")], "day30")
#> Error:
#> ! The validation data is missing 1 covariate that the model was developed with: sysbp.

# a forest that only predicts classes (fitted without probability = TRUE)
fit_class <- ranger::ranger(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse,
                            data = dev, num.trees = 100, seed = 1)
nb(fit_class, val, "day30")
#> Error:
#> ! Could not get predicted risks from this ranger model (You must set the argument probability=TRUE in the call to ranger in order to use predictRisk.ranger.). If a covariate is missing from the data, add it. Otherwise give `predict_function = function(model, newdata, horizon, cause)` to nb(), returning the risk of the event, or add a predict_risk() method for this class (see ?predict_risk).

# predictions outside [0, 1] are not probabilities
nb(lm(day30 ~ age + Killip, data = dev), val, "day30")
#> Error:
#> ! The model returned values outside [0, 1] (from -0.0874 to 0.528), so these are not probabilities. They may be scores from the model (e.g. log-odds, relative risks or predicted times) that must be turned into probabilities first.

Options of plot_dca()

Argument What it does
x, ... One or more results of nb(). Results drawn together must come from the same data, outcome and thresholds (voipred checks this).
type "nb": decision curve with Treat All and Treat None (default). "delta": \(\Delta NB\) of each model, with a dashed line at 0.
labels Names of the curves, one per result. Default: the label of each result.

See ?plot_dca for details. The plot is a ggplot object, so it can be changed with + or saved with ggplot2::ggsave():

p <- plot_dca(res_glm, res_rf, labels = c("Logistic regression", "Forest"))
p + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 0.2), ylim = c(-0.005, 0.07))

Part 2: survival outcome

Data

The Rotterdam breast cancer data (from the survival package). The outcome is death, with time in years; we evaluate the risk of death by 5 years.

rott <- rotterdam
rott$years <- rott$dtime / 365.25
set.seed(1)
j <- sample(nrow(rott))
sdev <- rott[j[1:1500], ]
sval <- rott[j[1501:nrow(rott)], ]

Net benefit of one model

The outcome is given with Surv() and the horizon is required:

fit_cox <- coxph(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes + grade + hormon + chemo,
                 data = sdev)

res_cox <- nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01), label = "Cox")
head(res_cox)
#> Net benefit of Cox (survival, horizon = 5, km): n = 1482, risk by horizon = 0.254, 6 thresholds
#>  threshold  NB_model    NB_all NB_none delta_NB
#>       0.00 0.2537089 0.2537089       0        0
#>       0.01 0.2461706 0.2461706       0        0
#>       0.02 0.2384785 0.2384785       0        0
#>       0.03 0.2306278 0.2306278       0        0
#>       0.04 0.2226135 0.2226135       0        0
#>       0.05 0.2144304 0.2144304       0        0

The columns are the same as for a binary outcome; the event is “death by 5 years”. The prevalence is the estimated risk of death by 5 years.

Plots

The same plot_dca() as for a binary outcome: the decision curve and delta_NB.

plot_dca(res_cox)

plot_dca(res_cox, type = "delta")

Comparing models

fit_aft <- survreg(Surv(years, death) ~ age + size + nodes, data = sdev,
                   dist = "weibull")
res_aft <- nb(fit_aft, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
              thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01), label = "Weibull AFT")

plot_dca(res_cox, res_aft)

plot_dca(res_cox, res_aft, type = "delta")

Options of nb() for a survival outcome

All the options of part 1 apply. In addition:

Argument What it does
outcome ~ Surv(time, status), with status 1 = event and 0 = censored. For competing risks, status is a factor whose first level is censoring (see below).
horizon The time by which the risk is predicted and the event counted (required), in the units of the survival times.
censoring How censoring is handled: "km" (default) or "cipcw" (see below).
cipcw With censoring = "cipcw": the censoring model or weights, made with cipcw_control().
cause Competing risks only: the event type of interest (default: the first event level).

See ?nb for the details of each argument.

Censoring: "km". The risk among the treated patients is a Kaplan-Meier estimate (Aalen-Johansen for competing risks), as in dcurves. It assumes that censoring is independent of the outcome. At a threshold where none of the treated patients is followed up to the horizon, the net benefit cannot be estimated: it is NA, with a warning.

Censoring: "cipcw". Conditional inverse probability of censoring weighting allows censoring to depend on covariates. Fit a model to the censoring times of the validation data, with censoring as the event (Surv(time, status == 0)), and give it with cipcw_control(). The censoring model can be any of the survival models voipred supports as prediction models (part 3), e.g. a Cox model, a parametric model or a random survival forest; for any other model, give its predict_function in cipcw_control(), or give the weights directly.

cens <- coxph(Surv(years, death == 0) ~ age + nodes + grade, data = sval)

res_cipcw <- nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5,
                thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                censoring = "cipcw", cipcw = cipcw_control(model = cens),
                label = "Cox")
plot_dca(res_cipcw)

plot_dca(res_cipcw, type = "delta")

Results with different censoring methods are different estimates, so plot_dca() does not draw them together.

The options of cipcw_control():

Argument What it does
model A survival model fitted to the censoring times of the validation data: any of the survival models voipred supports (part 3).
predict_function Optional: your own function giving the probability of remaining uncensored, for a censoring model voipred cannot predict from.
weight_event, weight_horizon Instead of a model: the censoring weights themselves, e.g. from a cross-fitted flexible model.
min_prob Optional truncation of small censoring probabilities (large weights). Off by default.
ties "left" (default) or "right": whether a censoring at exactly a patient’s own time counts.

See ?cipcw_control for the details.

Competing risks

With competing risks, the status is a factor whose first level is censoring and whose other levels are the event types. Here the events are recurrence and death, whichever comes first, and the model is a cause-specific Cox model:

crdat <- function(d) {
  d$cr_time   <- ifelse(d$recur == 1, d$rtime, d$dtime) / 365.25
  d$cr_code   <- ifelse(d$recur == 1, 1, ifelse(d$death == 1, 2, 0))
  d$cr_status <- factor(d$cr_code, 0:2, c("censored", "recurrence", "death"))
  d
}
sdev <- crdat(sdev)
sval <- crdat(sval)

fit_csc <- riskRegression::CSC(prodlim::Hist(cr_time, cr_code) ~ age + size + nodes + grade,
                               data = sdev)
res_csc <- nb(fit_csc, sval, ~ Surv(cr_time, cr_status), horizon = 5,
              cause = "recurrence", thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
              label = "Cause-specific Cox")
head(res_csc)
#> Net benefit of Cause-specific Cox (competing, cause = recurrence, horizon = 5, km): n = 1482, risk by horizon = 0.404, 6 thresholds
#>  threshold  NB_model    NB_all NB_none delta_NB
#>       0.00 0.4039649 0.4039649       0        0
#>       0.01 0.3979444 0.3979444       0        0
#>       0.02 0.3918010 0.3918010       0        0
#>       0.03 0.3855309 0.3855309       0        0
#>       0.04 0.3791301 0.3791301       0        0
#>       0.05 0.3725947 0.3725947       0        0
plot_dca(res_csc)

plot_dca(res_csc, type = "delta")

The net benefit is for “recurrence by 5 years”: a patient who died first counts as not having the event.

cIPCW works with competing risks in the same way. Only true censoring is censoring: the censoring model is fitted with the censored patients as the events (cr_status == "censored"), and patients with a competing event are not censored. voipred stops if the censoring model was fitted to one of the causes instead.

cens_cr <- coxph(Surv(cr_time, cr_status == "censored") ~ age + nodes + grade,
                 data = sval)

res_csc_cipcw <- nb(fit_csc, sval, ~ Surv(cr_time, cr_status), horizon = 5,
                    cause = "recurrence", thresholds = seq(0, 0.6, by = 0.01),
                    censoring = "cipcw", cipcw = cipcw_control(model = cens_cr),
                    label = "Cause-specific Cox")
plot_dca(res_csc_cipcw)

plot_dca(res_csc_cipcw, type = "delta")

Part 3: which models work

Models voipred supports

voipred gets the predicted risks from the fitted model itself: the probability of the event (binary), of the event by the horizon (survival), or of the cause by the horizon (competing risks). For the following models this works without anything else, and each is tested against the model’s own predictions:

  • Binary: glm (logit, probit, cloglog), logistf, mgcv::gam, earth, rpart, partykit::ctree, randomForest, ranger (probability = TRUE), gbm, xgboost, lightgbm, catboost, glmnet, cv.glmnet, e1071::svm (probability = TRUE), e1071::naiveBayes, naivebayes, nnet, MASS::lda, MASS::qda, kknn, and bayespred (bpmfit, bpm).
  • Survival: coxph, rms::cph, survreg, rms::psm, flexsurvreg, flexsurvspline, rstpm2::stpm2, mgcv::gam (cox.ph()), ranger, randomForestSRC, aorsf, partykit::ctree, prodlim, and bayespred.dev Bayesian Cox and parametric survival models.
  • Competing risks: riskRegression::CSC, riskRegression::FGR, cmprsk::crr, competing-risks randomForestSRC, and survival’s multi-state coxph.
  • Censoring models (cIPCW): the same survival models as above, fitted to the censoring times. voipred gets from them the probability of remaining uncensored, for survival and competing-risks outcomes alike.

“Supported” means only that voipred knows how to get predicted probabilities from the fitted model. It says nothing about whether the model is a good one, which is what the net benefit is for. Any other model whose predict() returns probabilities in the usual way, or that has a riskRegression::predictRisk() method, works too. See ?predict_risk for how the risks are obtained.

Any other model: predict_function

For a model voipred cannot predict from, give predict_function: a function of (model, newdata, horizon, cause) that returns one predicted risk per row of newdata. voipred calls it once, with newdata = data. It is optional: voipred uses its own route by default, and predict_function only when you give it, in which case it always replaces voipred’s own route.

A binary example (an SVM, which voipred also handles by itself):

fit_svm <- e1071::svm(factor(day30) ~ age + Killip + sysbp + pulse, data = dev,
                      probability = TRUE)
vars <- c("age", "Killip", "sysbp", "pulse")
nb(fit_svm, val, "day30", thresholds = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
   predict_function = function(model, newdata, ...) {
     pr <- predict(model, newdata[, vars], probability = TRUE)
     attr(pr, "probabilities")[, "1"]
   })
#> Net benefit of fit_svm: n = 5000, prevalence = 0.0692, 3 thresholds
#>  threshold    NB_model      NB_all NB_none     delta_NB
#>       0.05 0.017052632  0.02021053       0 -0.003157895
#>       0.10 0.007622222 -0.03422222       0  0.007622222
#>       0.20 0.004350000 -0.16350000       0  0.004350000

A survival example: the function receives the horizon and returns the risk of the event by then (here from survfit(), for illustration):

nb(fit_cox, sval, ~ Surv(years, death), horizon = 5, thresholds = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
   predict_function = function(model, newdata, horizon, ...) {
     sf <- survfit(model, newdata = newdata)
     1 - as.vector(summary(sf, times = horizon)$surv)
   })
#> Net benefit of fit_cox (survival, horizon = 5, km): n = 1482, risk by horizon = 0.254, 3 thresholds
#>  threshold   NB_model      NB_all NB_none      delta_NB
#>        0.1 0.17028932  0.17078769       0 -0.0004983712
#>        0.2 0.11529191  0.06713616       0  0.0481557545
#>        0.3 0.06554028 -0.06613011       0  0.0655402787

The function’s output is checked like any other: it must be one probability per patient, in [0, 1], and not only 0s and 1s. A censoring model can be given its own predict_function in the same way, in cipcw_control().
